newsitem.title: GERMANY: German upturn still not backed by investment - banks.
newsitem.headline: German upturn still not backed by investment - banks.

text.p: Germany's economic recovery is not yet assured because investment remains stagnant, partly because of lack of coherent economic policy-making, a German banking group said on Friday.

Despite a return to respectable economic growth of 1.5 percent in the second quarter it was too early to sound the all-clear on the upturn, the Federal Association of German Banks said in a statement.

The strong growth in the second quarter and recent signs of an upturn in business confidence have prompted the German government to issue a revised forecast for full-year economic growth of up to one percent.

But the association said that experience showed that a cyclical upturn quickly lost momentum unless it was backed by investment. It noted that building investment was falling and there was no sign whatsoever of a rise in spending on plant and equipment.
Capital spending was stagnating partly because of high costs, inadequate earnings prospects, surplus industrial capacity and weak consumer spending amid high unemployment, the group said.
"A further decisive reason for the gloomy investment climate can be found in economic policy," the statement said.
"It continues to send out very conflicting signals which increase the risk to investors and unsettle consumers as well."

Uncertainty remained over whether the government would be able to push through plans for sweeping tax reforms, currently opposed by the Social Democrat-led upper house of the German parliament, the statement said.
It was also unclear whether corporate taxes would be cut next year.

"The fact that the debate on the planned income tax reform is being conducted without clear outlines -- even before the commission convened for this purpose has submitted its proposals -- does not contribute to clarifying the outlook for the future tax burden," the statement said.

But it added that last Friday's parliamentary approval of the government's austerity package of spending cuts should boost public confidence. The package aims to cut public spending by 70 billion narks in next year's budget.
The group also called on unions to maintain the wage restraint they had shown this year.
